questions.prompt: Which certificate in a chain does your browser trust without checking a signature?

choices.label: The root certificate, because it is already installed on the computer
The intermediate certificate, because it signs the others
The website's own certificate, because it names the site

questions.prompt: You are looking at a certificate and want to know whether it is a root. What tells you?

choices.label: Its subject and its issuer are the same, and its own key signed it
It has the word Root in its name
It is valid for far longer than an ordinary certificate

questions.prompt: You made a certificate with the common name localhost, but the browser still says the name does not match. What did it actually want?

choices.label: The subject alternative name, which is the only name field browsers trust
The common name spelled differently
A serial number matching the website

questions.prompt: A certificate says it was issued by your root. What proves that your root really issued it?

choices.label: The signature on it, which only your root's private key could have made
The issuer name matching your root's subject name
The two files sitting in the same folder

questions.prompt: Your certificate is served correctly and has the right name, and the browser still shows a full-page warning. Why?

choices.label: The browser does not trust the root that signed it
A certificate you made yourself is always treated as expired
Browsers refuse any certificate that was not bought

questions.prompt: You added your root to the trust list, restarted the browser, and the padlock appeared. What changed about the certificate?

choices.label: Nothing at all. Only who the browser is willing to trust changed
It was signed again, this time by an authority the browser knows
The browser upgraded it to a trusted certificate

questions.prompt: You trusted your root on Windows and Chrome is happy, but Firefox still warns about the same page. Why?

choices.label: Firefox keeps its own list of trusted roots and never reads the operating system's
Firefox has cached the old warning and needs its cache cleared
Firefox does not support certificates you make yourself

questions.prompt: Your trust list shows a root called My Root, but the page is still refused. You have been through the lesson twice. What tells you whether the trusted one is the right one?

choices.label: Comparing fingerprints, which are different for every certificate even when the names match
The name, since two roots cannot share one
The dates, since the browser always uses the newest one

questions.prompt: In the setup you built, where does the encryption stop?

choices.label: At the proxy. Everything behind it speaks plain http
At the backend, which decrypts the request it is given
Nowhere. The whole path stays encrypted end to end

questions.prompt: The backend received a plain http request carrying X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Why does that header exist?

choices.label: The backend cannot tell the original request was encrypted, so the proxy tells it
It tells the backend to encrypt its reply
The browser sets it so servers know it wants https

questions.prompt: The backend reported the request as coming from 172.29.0.3, not from your computer. Why?

choices.label: The connection the backend sees is the proxy's; your browser never spoke to the backend
Docker replaces every address with a made-up one
https hides the visitor's address from the server

questions.prompt: What is the main reason to put ten services behind one reverse proxy?

choices.label: One place deals with certificates, and the ten services never need to know about them
Requests are faster because the proxy caches every reply
Each service can then have its own certificate

questions.prompt: Your computer trusts your root and the browser shows a padlock, but a Java program connecting to the same address fails. Why?

choices.label: Java keeps its own list of trusted roots and does not read the operating system's
Java refuses certificates that were not bought from an authority
Java caches trust decisions until the machine is restarted

questions.prompt: Java stops with "unable to find valid certification path to requested target". What has actually happened?

choices.label: Java followed the chain up to your root and did not find it in its own list
The certificate is malformed and could not be read
Java could not reach the server to fetch the rest of the chain

questions.prompt: Which file do you import with keytool so a Java program will accept your site?

choices.label: The root certificate, because that is what Java needs to decide who to trust
The certificate for localhost, because that is the one being served
The root's private key, so Java can check the signature itself
Which certificates this program is willing to accept as the start of a chain
Which certificate this program shows when something connects to it
Which kinds of encryption this program will agree to use
